definition: Producing a large amount of money or profit.
example: The fishing village found that renting rooms to summer visitors was more lucrative than hauling nets.
nuance: Profitable can mean earning any profit at all, while lucrative stresses that the money earned is large; don't confuse it with ludicrous.
prompt: A baker is deciding whether she can afford to open a second shop.
options: Catering weddings proved so lucrative that the baker could afford a second shop.
Her lucrative side business lost money every single month until she finally shut it down.
The baker told a lucrative joke that left everyone at the counter laughing.
After a long nap, the baker felt lucrative and ready to knead dough.
reasons: The catering brought in enough money to pay for expansion, which is exactly the point of the word.
A venture that loses money every month is the reverse of one that pays well.
This confuses the word with ludicrous; a joke that gets laughs earns nothing.
The word describes jobs or ventures that earn money, not how a person feels.

practice.prompt: A high school student is comparing summer jobs before choosing one.
options: The manager's lucrative explanation cleared up every question she had about her schedule.
The lucrative July heat made her want to stay indoors with a fan.
Lifeguarding was the most lucrative choice, paying nearly double the library job.
Walking the neighbors' dogs for free turned out to be her most lucrative summer job of all.
reasons: This mixes the word up with lucid; a clear explanation is not a source of income.
Hot weather earns no money, so the adjective has nothing to describe here.
A job that pays far more than the others earns this description.
Unpaid work can't be the best-paying option, so the sentence contradicts itself.
